So, Ana, you are really coming to Oslo in January? You are a brave woman.
I am! Tell me the truth. What should I pack?
Well, you might want to bring wool socks. Actually, you'd better bring two pairs.
Two pairs? Is that a Norwegian rule of thumb?
Sort of. And at my parents' house you have to take your shoes off at the door. It is not optional.
Do I have to bring a gift? In Brazil, you never arrive with empty hands.
You don't have to bring anything big. Flowers or chocolate is perfect. But you mustn't be late. Dinner at six means six.
Dinner at six? In Brazil we eat at nine! But okay, when in Rome. I will be there at five to six.

My name is Ingrid, and I live in Bergen, on the west coast of Norway. People always ask me about the rules of a Norwegian home, so here they are. First, you have to take your shoes off at the door. Nobody will tell you, but everybody will look at your feet. Second, you don't have to bring a big present. A small thing is perfect, and something too expensive can make people uncomfortable. Third, if dinner is at six, you should arrive at six. Not at ten past six, and please, not at a quarter to. And one more thing. When a Norwegian gives you advice, it sounds very soft. We say, maybe you could, or it might be an idea to. My Brazilian friend Camila did not understand that at first. I told her, it might be an idea to bring a warmer coat. She thought it was a small suggestion. It was minus twelve that week. She learned.

Hello, I am Arjun, from Pune, in India. In my family, advice is very direct. My aunt says, you must eat more, you are too thin. You should call your mother every day. You have to come for lunch on Sunday. For a foreigner, this sounds like orders. For us, it is love. If my aunt does not tell me what to do, I think she is angry with me. Then I went to study in Manchester, in England, and everything was upside down. In my first week, my landlady said, you might want to put the bins out on Thursday night. I thought, okay, it is optional. I did not do it. On Friday she knocked on my door, very politely, and said, the bins really must go out on Thursday. So in India, must can be love. In England, might want to can be a rule. Now, when an English person gives me soft advice, I always follow it.
